units.name: Making Sentences
units.summary: What makes a sentence complete, and how to start and end it.

topics.name: Complete Sentences
topics.summary: Every sentence needs a who and a what-they-did.

objectives.text: Tell a complete sentence from an incomplete one.
Start a sentence with a capital letter.
End a sentence with a full stop or a question mark.

keyTerms.definition: A group of words that tells a whole idea.
A big letter, like A or B, used to start a sentence.
The dot at the end of a sentence. It tells the reader to stop.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
A sentence must tell a whole idea.

You will learn what a sentence needs.

You will learn how to start it and how to end it.

sections.heading: A sentence needs two things
sections.body:
Every sentence needs a WHO and a WHAT THEY DID.

Look at this:

    The dog

That is not a sentence. You know who. But what did the dog do? You are still waiting.

Now look at this:

    The dog barked.

Now it is a sentence. There is a who — the dog. There is what it did — barked.

The idea is whole. You are not left waiting.
sections.example:
Finding what is missing.

    ran to the river

What did? A boy? A goat? You do not know. The WHO is missing.

Add it:

    The boy ran to the river.

Now it is a sentence.

Another one:

    My little sister

You know who. But she did what? The WHAT is missing.

Add it:

    My little sister sang a song.

Now it is a sentence.

sections.heading: Start big, end with a dot
sections.body:
Every sentence starts with a capital letter.

    the rain fell        ← wrong. Small t.
    The rain fell.       ← right. Big T.

Every sentence ends with a mark.

If you are telling something, use a full stop:

    The rain fell.

If you are asking something, use a question mark:

    Did the rain fall?

The capital letter tells the reader "a sentence starts here". The mark at the end tells them "it stops here".

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
Say whether each one is a complete sentence. If it is not, say what is missing.

1. The baby cried.

2. under the big tree

3. My mother cooks rice.

4. The three goats

5. Now write this properly, with a capital letter and a full stop:  the sun is hot

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• A sentence tells a whole idea.
• It needs a who and a what-they-did.
• Start it with a capital letter.
• End it with a full stop, or a question mark if you are asking.

questions.question: Which one is a complete sentence?
questions.explanation: A sentence needs a WHO and a WHAT THEY DID. "The baby cried." has both — the baby, and what the baby did. The others leave you waiting: "My three goats" tells you who but never says what they did.

questions.question: What is missing from this: "ran to the river"?
questions.explanation: You know what happened — running. But WHO ran? A boy? A goat? The who is missing. Add it and you have a sentence: "The boy ran to the river."

questions.question: How should you write this properly:  the sun is hot
questions.explanation: A sentence needs BOTH things: a capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end. "The sun is hot" has the capital but no full stop, so it is not finished.
